parts:
I asked my partner to find some partner in collaborations that we could partner with that are actively in MedSpa's and have thousands of MedSpa's they work with and maybe sell a product, a laser a machine, something that their reps for or that they work in tandem with and I wanted him to find people like that that he gave me this list which is not what I wanted. Please help me construct a message to him letting him know exactly the people that I was talking about: Category C: Private-Label Manufacturer Partnership Targets
Ranked by fit for a TLC referral/preferred-vendor relationship — July 2026
Ranking methodology: Each company is scored on three things: (1) whether there's a real named contact whose job is to evaluate partnerships (not just a founder wearing every hat), (2) whether their business model and account minimums actually fit TLC's $1M+ ARR med spa client base, and (3) narrative/credibility fit with how TLC positions itself. A company can rank lower for being too small or informal to reliably support a real channel program, even if they'd say yes fast.

Tier 1: Strongest Match
1. Cosmetic Solutions (CSIL)
Website: naturalskincare.com Contact: Matt Unger, President & Chief Commercial Officer Why #1: The title alone is the tell — "Chief Commercial Officer" means partnerships and channel deals are literally his job, not something bolted onto a founder's plate. Scale backs it up: 100,000 sq. ft. Boca Raton campus, a newly named CEO (John Puckett, since the announcement) signaling active growth investment, and a real Business Development Executive function that shows up at trade shows courting exactly this kind of relationship. Caveat: $20,000 opening order minimum and 500 units/SKU. That's steep for a boutique med spa, but it's a near-perfect filter for TLC's actual ICP. A med spa that can't clear that bar probably isn't ready for a serious private-label launch anyway.
2. Vitelle Labs
Website: vitellelab.com Contact: Aleks Vranicic, VP of Sales & Technical Training Why #2: Nearly 30 years in business, described as the manufacturing partner used by national skincare brands, plastic surgeons, and dermatologists, not just spas. Vranicic's title covers both sales and training, meaning he's built for exactly the kind of onboarding a referred client would need. Also more accessible than CSIL: entry programs start around $500, so it can serve a wider band of your client roster, not just your biggest accounts.
3. Sarati International
Website: saratiprivatelabel.com Contact: David Privett, Account Manager (CEO Barbara Creighton as backup/escalation) Why #3: Founded 1992, genuinely established, and one of the few on this list with an actual "Account Manager" title, meaning relationship management is a defined function, not an afterthought. Smaller team than Vitelle or CSIL (roughly 11–20 employees), which is why it sits at #3 rather than higher, but still a legitimate, durable manufacturer.


Tier 2: Strong Founder-Led Fit
4. Trilogy Laboratories
Website: trilogylaboratories.com Contact: Dr. Kristen Flaharty, Owner & Founder Why #4: The best narrative fit on this entire list. Flaharty built Trilogy because she couldn't find a private-label partner in small enough quantities for her husband's own med spa (Azul Medical Spa) — an operator solving her own operator problem, which mirrors Bethany's story almost exactly. That's a genuinely strong basis for a founder-to-founder conversation. It ranks below Tier 1 only because it's a smaller company (~$3M revenue) run through a "Project Consultant" team rather than a dedicated commercial exec, so the partnership conversation may move slower and less formally.
5. Induction Therapies
Website: inductiontherapies.com Contact: Angelia Inscoe, Founder Why #5: 30+ years of formulation experience, an FDA-inspected facility, and explicit focus on post-treatment/protocol products — directly relevant given how often post-procedure care comes up in your client work. Assigns a "dedicated representative" to accounts, which is a good sign for ongoing relationship management even without a named commercial exec.
6. AMP Medical
Website: ampaesthetics.com Contact: Peter Marchese & Elle Marchese, Founders Why #6: Strong client testimonials and an existing model of ongoing sales support (a resident medical aesthetician who trains client staff). Ranks here rather than higher because there's less public information confirming scale, and because of the real risk of confusing this company with two or three unrelated firms that also go by "AMP" in the aesthetics space. Double-check you're on ampaesthetics.com in any reply thread.


Tier 3: Legitimate but Smaller
7. Global Beauty Private Label
Website: globalbeauty.net Contact: Ellen Clark, L.E., MA, Founder Why #7: Over a decade in business with real physician and med spa recognition nationwide, but public information on scale, team size, and process is thin. Worth pursuing, just with less certainty going in than Tiers 1–2.
8. Pravada
Website: pravadaprivatelabel.com Contact: Marlene Thompson, President Why #8: Low MOQ and genuinely welcoming to new brands, but reported revenue (~$789K) is modest, which raises real questions about whether they have the bandwidth to support a formal, ongoing referral program at any real volume. Good option to have in your back pocket for smaller or newer clients rather than a flagship recommendation.


Tier 4: Weakest Fit — Approach With Lower Expectations
9. Ataliene
Website: atalieneskincare.com Contact: No named leader found (RocketReach lists 2 employees). Use sales@atalieneskincare.com. Why #9: Small enough that whoever answers your email is probably a decision-maker, which cuts both ways: potentially fast and personal, but there's no real infrastructure behind it. Treat this as a relationship experiment, not a cornerstone partner.
10. Medical Spa Supply
Website: medicalspasupply.com Contact: No named leader found. Use the general contact form. Why #10: Private label is one offering within a broader general-distributor identity (they also show up in the wholesale distributor category), not their core specialty. No visible decision-maker for a partnership conversation makes this a lower-confidence target.
11. Blanka
Website: blankabrand.com Contact: No named leader found. Use the general contact form. Why #11 (last): Blanka is built as a subscription/dropship platform for solo estheticians and small independent brands launching their first line, not medical-grade, $1M+ ARR med spas. It's the clearest ICP mismatch on this list. I'd deprioritize this one unless a client specifically asks about the DTC/subscription model.



Compiled from public web research as of July 2026 (company websites, press releases, LinkedIn, and business data aggregators). Leadership and contact details in this space turn over — confirm before finalizing outreach, particularly for Tiers 3–4 where no named contact was publicly available.

Here’s a clear message you can send him:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="68421"}
I think there was a misunderstanding about the type of partnership targets I was asking you to find.

I was not looking for private-label skincare manufacturers or companies we could simply refer clients to as preferred vendors. Most of the companies on this list do not already have meaningful access to thousands of med spas, which is the entire point of the partnership strategy.

I am looking for established companies that already work directly with a large number of med spas and have sales reps, account managers, trainers, consultants, or educators actively inside these practices every day.

Think companies that sell:

• Lasers and aesthetic devices  
• Body contouring machines  
• Injectables or aesthetic products  
• Medical-grade skincare lines  
• Peptides, wellness products, or weight-loss programs  
• Med spa software, EMRs, CRMs, financing, or payment processing  
• Training, compliance, insurance, or staffing solutions specifically for med spas  
• Large distributors that supply thousands of aesthetic practices  

Examples would be companies like Allergan Aesthetics, Galderma, Merz, Evolus, SkinCeuticals, ZO Skin Health, Hydrafacial, Sciton, Alma, InMode, Cartessa, Candela, PatientNow, RepeatMD, Boulevard, or large aesthetic distributors and buying groups.

I am not necessarily asking us to partner with those exact companies. Those are examples of the type and scale of company I mean.

The ideal partner already has relationships with hundreds or thousands of med spa owners, but they are not directly competing with our end-to-end growth services. Their reps may hear med spa owners say things like:

“We bought the machine, but we are not getting enough patients for it.”

“Our membership is not working.”

“We need better marketing.”

“Our front desk is not converting the leads.”

“We are not retaining the patients we bring in.”

That is where TLC becomes valuable to both sides.

They can introduce TLC to practices that need help generating demand, improving conversion, filling treatment schedules, selling memberships, and retaining patients. In return, we can recommend their products, equipment, software, or services to qualified TLC clients when there is a legitimate fit.

I want you to identify the actual partnership decision-makers inside those companies, such as:

• VP of Strategic Partnerships  
• VP of Business Development  
• Director of Channel Partnerships  
• National Sales Director  
• Director of Practice Development  
• Head of Provider Partnerships  
• Regional or National Account Director  

The research should answer:

1. How many med spas or aesthetic practices do they currently serve?
2. What do they sell?
3. Do they have reps or account managers who regularly interact with med spa owners?
4. What problems do their customers experience after buying their product or service?
5. How could TLC help their customers become more successful?
6. What would make the partnership financially or strategically valuable to them?
7. Who is the specific person we should contact about a national referral, affiliate, co-marketing, or channel partnership?

The private-label companies may be useful later as client resources, but they are not the high-level strategic collaboration partners I was asking you to research.
:::

This gives him the distinction between a vendor list and an actual audience-access partnership strategy.
